notes.meaning: Elisha delivers a message of sudden hope from the Lord to the king and his court. Within twenty-four hours, the deadly famine in Samaria will end, and flour and barley will sell at cheap market prices right at the city gate. Even after the king had blamed God and threatened Elisha, God chose to show mercy to his starving people.

The king's chief officer scoffs at the promise, saying this could not happen even if God opened floodgates in the sky. Elisha responds that the officer will see the food with his own eyes but will not eat a single bite of it. Proud unbelief insults God and cuts people off from his blessings.

Four men with leprosy were forced to sit outside the city gate, cut off from the community because of their skin disease. No food was coming out of the besieged city to sustain them. They realized that sitting still meant they would soon starve to death.

The men weighed their choices and saw that entering the city or staying at the gate led to the exact same fate. Their only chance of survival was to surrender to the enemy camp. If the soldiers killed them, they would die anyway, but if they showed mercy, the men would live.

The lepers set out at evening dusk and made their way to the edge of the Aramean camp. When they arrived where the enemy guards should have been, not a single person was there. The camp was totally quiet and abandoned.

God had caused the Arameans to hear the terrifying sound of a huge army with horses and chariots charging toward them. In their panic, the soldiers assumed the king of Israel had hired armies from the north and south to crush them. God delivered his people by striking fear into the enemy without Israel lifting a weapon.

Overcome with terror, the Aramean soldiers fled on foot in the evening dusk. They were so desperate to escape that they left their tents, horses, donkeys, and all their gear untouched. Their sudden panic left behind a camp fully stocked with food and riches.

The four lepers stepped into a tent and ate and drank until they were satisfied. After satisfying their hunger, they gathered silver, gold, and fine clothes and went out to bury them. Then they entered another tent and hid more treasures for themselves.

The lepers soon felt guilty for hoarding the wealth while their fellow citizens were starving. They recognized that this was a day of good news, and keeping silent until morning would bring guilt and punishment on them. They decided to return immediately and share the good news with the king's palace.

The men returned to the city gate and called out to the watchmen on duty. They reported that the enemy camp was completely deserted, with tents left standing and horses and donkeys still tied up. Because they could not enter the city as lepers, they shouted what they knew to the guards.
The gatekeepers shouted the report from person to person until it passed into the city. The joyful news quickly reached the royal household inside the palace.

The king woke up during the night but refused to believe the good news. He assumed the Arameans were playing a military trick, hiding in the fields so they could ambush the starving citizens as soon as they came out. His fear and suspicion made him blind to God's promise.

One of the king's servants advised sending scouts out on a few of the city's few remaining horses. He argued that the scouts had nothing to lose, since remaining in the city would bring the same death by starvation as everyone else was facing. Investigating the camp was worth the small risk.
The men prepared two chariots with horses, and the king ordered them to track the enemy. He wanted clear evidence before allowing his people to leave the safety of the walls.

The scouts tracked the retreat all the way to the Jordan River. Along the whole road, they found clothes and weapons that the Arameans had tossed away to run faster. The messengers returned and assured the king that the enemy had truly fled in panic.

When the scouts confirmed the news, the starving crowd poured out of the city and looted the enemy camp. Suddenly, fine flour and barley were sold at the gate for small, cheap prices, exactly as the Lord had declared through Elisha. God's promise proved completely true.

The king placed his trusted officer in charge of the city gate to keep order among the crowd. But the hungry multitude rushed forward so violently that the officer was knocked down and crushed to death. This fulfilled the exact judgment Elisha had spoken to him the day before.

The story looks back to show how perfectly the prophet's words came to pass. Elisha had named the exact day, the exact place, and the exact price for both barley and fine flour. Nothing that God promised failed to happen.

The writer also reminds the reader of the officer's mocking words about windows in heaven. Elisha had warned him directly that he would witness the miracle but never enjoy it. God's word answered the man's scoffing with absolute truth.

The officer died under the feet of the rushing crowd, precisely as Elisha had spoken. He saw the abundance with his eyes, but judgment overtook him before he could taste any of it. God's warnings against mockers are just as certain as his promises to save.
